summary: Children aged 7–9 build and reason about polar food chains. Antarctic: phytoplankton → krill → fish/penguins → leopard seals/orcas; Arctic: ice algae → zooplankton → fish → seals → polar bears. Core ideas: every chain begins at a sunlight-powered producer; the arrow means 'is eaten by / energy flows to' (points toward the eater); tiny organisms (plankton, krill) are the load-bearing base; and removing a small link ripples up to the biggest predators. The primary activity is constructing a chain and perturbing it; order/arrow-direction checks and a conversational hook are companions or scaffolds with narrower purposes.
misconceptions: The arrow points from predator to prey — it points from the eaten to the eater (energy flows up)
Big animals are the most important — the tiny producers and krill actually support everything above them
Food chains start with an animal — they start with a producer powered by sunlight (plankton/algae)
Removing one small link doesn't matter — losing krill or plankton can collapse the whole chain
Arctic and Antarctic have totally different food systems — both follow the same producer→consumer→predator pattern

activities.title: Build a polar chain and pull out the krill
steps: From a jumbled set of organism cards or on-screen tokens, place the producer first at the base — phytoplankton, marked with a little sun icon to show it is powered by sunlight.
Add krill, then a penguin, then a leopard seal, drawing or snapping an arrow between each pair.

Read each arrow aloud as 'is eaten by / energy flows to': 'phytoplankton is eaten by krill', 'krill is eaten by penguin', 'penguin is eaten by leopard seal'. If an arrow is pointing the wrong way, flip it so it points toward the eater.

Once the chain is complete, remove the krill and trace out loud what happens up this chain: the penguin runs short of food, then the leopard seal that eats penguins also goes hungry. (Real penguins and seals can eat some other foods, but krill are a major food for many Antarctic animals.)
State in your own words why the smallest organism can matter most to the whole chain.
activities.insight: In polar seas the tiniest producers and krill hold up the largest predators; arrows carry energy upward from the sunlit base, and losing a small link cascades all the way to the top.

activities.title: Compare the two poles side by side
steps: Build or lay out the Antarctic chain (phytoplankton → krill → penguin/fish → leopard seal/orca) and the Arctic chain (ice algae → zooplankton → fish → seal → polar bear) next to each other.
Toggle or point between them and name, for each, the producer, a consumer, and a top predator.
Describe the shared shape: producer → consumer → predator, with a tiny sunlight-powered organism at every base.
activities.insight: Both poles follow the same producer→consumer→predator pattern, so the two systems are parallel, not wholly different.

activities.title: Order-the-chain and arrow-direction check
steps: Given a scrambled set of polar organisms, arrange them in order from producer to top predator.
Choose which way each arrow should point and justify it using the 'is eaten by / energy flows to' rule.
Answer: at the very start of a polar food chain, what kind of organism is it, and why does something so tiny matter so much?
activities.insight: Sequence and arrow direction can be checked quickly, consolidating the vocabulary of producer, consumer and predator.

activities.title: Interview a krill (spoken hook)
steps: Role-play a short interview with a krill 'holding up the whole Antarctic', asking who depends on it and what would happen if it vanished.
Have the krill explain where it gets its own energy (eating phytoplankton, which is powered by the sun).
After the hook, move to building and perturbing a real chain to test the claims made in the interview.
activities.insight: A playful voice can motivate the idea that the smallest organism supports the whole web, before the learner tests it by construction.

checkQuestion: Here is an Antarctic food chain shown with arrows: phytoplankton → krill → penguin → leopard seal. A student reads it as 'the leopard seal is the most important because it's biggest, and the arrows show who eats who — pointing from the eater to its food.' Which way do the arrows really point, and if all the tiny krill vanished, what would happen to the seals and penguins — why?
checkAnswer: The arrows point from the food to the EATER — they show the direction energy flows (phytoplankton are eaten BY krill, krill BY penguins, penguins BY leopard seals), so the arrow points toward whoever does the eating, not toward the prey. And the tiny organisms at the START (phytoplankton and krill) are the foundation of everything: if the krill vanished, the penguins would lose their main food and crash, and the leopard seals and orcas above them would starve too. The smallest creatures, not the biggest, hold the whole chain up.
